fixes.answer: Yes, I think overconsumption is a defining feature of modern society. We are constantly [[bombarded]] with advertising designed to create desires for things we do not truly need. Cheap goods and easy credit make impulsive buying effortless. Many people also shop for emotional reasons, as a form of therapy. So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by [[manufactured]] wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite [[wasteful]].

Online shopping has [[revolutionised]] the experience. It offers [[unparalleled]] convenience, allowing people to buy almost anything from home at any hour, with easy price comparison. This has, however, put pressure on traditional physical shops, many of which have struggled. The experience has become more efficient but arguably less social. So while the internet has made shopping far more convenient and accessible, it has also transformed our [[high streets]], not always for the better.

Advertising is influential because it is sophisticated and [[pervasive]]. It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which [[reinforces]] its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly [[steering]] our behaviour.

Consumerism has a profound and mixed impact. It drives economic growth and provides jobs, which is beneficial. However, it also fuels [[materialism]], encouraging people to equate happiness with possessions, which many would argue is [[illusory]]. It contributes significantly to environmental degradation through waste and [[resource depletion]]. It can also foster debt and dissatisfaction. So while it powers the economy, unchecked consumerism carries serious social and environmental costs.
fixes.why: 'environmental' and 'costs' are plain; marked 'materialism' and 'resource depletion'; softened 'studies suggest'

fixes.answer: I am cautiously hopeful. There is a growing awareness of the environmental and ethical impact of our purchases, and movements towards [[minimalism]], sustainability and ethical consumption are [[gaining momentum]]. Younger generations in particular seem more [[values-driven]] in their spending. However, the powerful forces of marketing and convenience remain strong. So while I believe conscious consumption will increase, whether it becomes the norm depends on a genuine cultural shift.
fixes.why: 'increase', 'norm', 'shift' are plain; kept 'values-driven' and marked 'minimalism' and 'gaining momentum'

fixes.answer: Education and awareness are key. Helping people understand the true environmental and social cost of their purchases can shift attitudes. Encouraging habits like buying quality over quantity, repairing rather than replacing, and choosing ethical brands makes a difference. Governments can also play a role through regulation and [[incentives]]. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a cultural value of [[sufficiency]] over excess, where we question whether we truly need something, is the most sustainable path.

The advantages are clear: convenience, a vast selection, easy price comparison and often lower prices, all from home. It is a great [[time-saver]]. The disadvantages include the inability to physically examine products before buying, delivery delays, the environmental cost of packaging and transport, and the temptation to [[overspend]]. It also lacks the social experience of physical shopping. So it offers wonderful convenience, but with some real [[trade-offs]] in experience and impact.

I only partly agree. There is undeniably a short-term thrill in acquiring something new, so buying can bring a [[fleeting]] sense of pleasure. However, many people feel this happiness is temporary and superficial, quickly fading in a cycle sometimes called the [[hedonic treadmill]]. Lasting happiness tends to come from experiences and relationships, not possessions. So while shopping offers momentary joy, relying on it for happiness is ultimately [[hollow]] and unfulfilling.
fixes.why: 4 marks; marked 'fleeting' and 'hedonic treadmill' instead of 'superficial' and 'unfulfilling'; softened 'extensive research suggests'
